teile.einleitung: Something is fair when everyone has the same chances and keeps to the rules. Fairness is important in games, in sport and wherever people do things together.
wichtigste: Fair means: the same rules and the same chances for everyone.
In a fair race everyone starts at the same time.
Fair behaviour in sport is called **fair play**.
Rolling dice gives everyone the same chance.
A foul is a breach of the rules of the game.
Fair winners stay friendly.

abschnitte.text: In a **race** everyone should set off at the same time. Anyone who starts too early gains an **unfair advantage**. That is not fair on the others. That is why there is a starting signal, for example ‘Ready, steady, go!’. That way everyone has the same chance of winning.

Sometimes you have to decide who goes first in a game. You can do this fairly, for example by **rolling a die**. When you roll a die, every child has the same chance. You can also toss a coin or say a counting-out rhyme. What matters is that nobody is favoured.

In sport, fair behaviour is called **fair play**. It means keeping to the rules and respecting your opponent. A **foul** is a breach of the rules, for example tripping someone up. There is a penalty for it, such as a free kick or a yellow card. The **referee** makes sure that everyone plays fairly.

Fair does not always mean that everyone does exactly the same thing. If a child cannot run because of a **plaster cast**, they can take on another job, for example timing or keeping score. That way they can still **join in**. It is fair when everyone can take part.

Whoever wins is happy. But a **fair winner** stays friendly and does not laugh at anyone. Whoever loses may be disappointed. A **good loser** still congratulates the winner. After a game people often shake hands. That way the fun lasts for everyone.

gewusst: In football there is the yellow card as a warning and the red card for sending a player off.
At many sporting events there is a special prize for especially fair behaviour.

teile.einleitung: The Golden Rule is one of the oldest and best-known principles of morality. It says: treat others as you would like to be treated yourself. It is found in many cultures and religions of the world.
wichtigste: The Golden Rule asks you to treat others as you would like to be treated yourself.
In German it is known as a rhyme: ‘Was du nicht willst, dass man dir tu, das füg auch keinem andern zu’ (what you do not want done to you, do not do to anyone else).
At its heart is a change of perspective: you put yourself in the other person's position.
Confucius was already teaching a form of the rule in China around 500 BC.
In the Bible it appears in the Sermon on the Mount in the Gospel of Matthew.
It appears in all the great world religions.
Kant's categorical imperative is often compared with it.

abschnitte.text: The Golden Rule is a rule of **reciprocity**. Before you act, you ask yourself: how would I feel if someone did this to me? This **change of perspective** is at its heart. There is a negative form, which says what you should not do, and a positive form, which calls on you to do good. The well-known German rhyme belongs to the negative form.

The Chinese thinker **Confucius** said, in essence: what you do not wish for yourself, do not do to others. Similar sayings are also found in **Judaism**, **Christianity**, **Islam**, **Hinduism** and **Buddhism**. In Judaism, for example, a saying of the scholar Hillel is well known: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. Because so many cultures know it, the Golden Rule is regarded as a principle shared by all humanity.

In the **Gospel of Matthew** (chapter 7, verse 12) Jesus says that you should do to others as you would like to be treated yourself. This passage belongs to the **Sermon on the Mount**, a long speech with important teachings. There is a similar passage in the Gospel of Luke. Here the rule is put positively: it calls on you to actively do good yourself.

The **principle of retaliation** says: tit for tat. Like is answered with like, including bad with bad. The Golden Rule goes further: you should take the first good step yourself, without waiting for the other person. With the **categorical imperative**, the philosopher **Immanuel Kant** developed a principle that is often compared with it. But Kant himself distinguished it from the Golden Rule.

The Golden Rule can be applied everywhere. If you show a new child round the school, you are doing what you would want in that situation yourself. When sharing, listening or comforting, too, the question helps: how would I like to be treated? This makes living together in the family, the class and the community friendlier.

gewusst: The Golden Rule is so old that nobody knows exactly who first put it into words.
Almost identical sayings arose in cultures that knew nothing of each other at the time, for example in China and in the Middle East.

teile.einleitung: Human dignity means that every person has a value that nobody may take away. It applies to everyone, however old, rich or ill they are, and wherever they come from. Many constitutions and human rights are built on it.
wichtigste: Human dignity means: every person has a value that nobody may take away.
Article 7 of the Federal Constitution reads: ‘Human dignity must be respected and protected.’
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights begins with the dignity of all people.
The German Basic Law begins: ‘Human dignity shall be inviolable.’
Immanuel Kant said that a person must never be treated merely as a means.
Torture violates human dignity especially seriously and is banned worldwide.
Henry Dunant helped to found the International Committee of the Red Cross.

abschnitte.text: **Human dignity** is the special value that every person has. You do not have to earn it, and you cannot lose it either. It applies to babies just as much as to old people, to the healthy as to the sick. Anyone who respects dignity does not treat others like objects. Nobody may be humiliated, laughed at or shown up.

The philosopher **Immanuel Kant** strongly shaped thinking about dignity. He said that a person must never be used **merely as a means**, but must always also be treated as an **end**. Things have a price and can be replaced. People, on the other hand, have a dignity that is above any price. This idea is found in many laws today.

Article 1 of the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** of 1948 begins like this: ‘All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.’ The German **Basic Law** of 1949 begins with the sentence: ‘Human dignity shall be inviolable.’ In the **Swiss Federal Constitution**, **Article 7** reads: ‘Human dignity must be respected and protected.’ All authorities at federal, cantonal and municipal level must abide by this.

**Torture** violates human dignity especially seriously. It is banned worldwide, among other things by a UN convention against torture. Slavery, exclusion and humiliation also violate dignity. In everyday life, respect begins with small things: not laughing at anyone, staying friendly and taking all people seriously.

abschnitte.titel: Henry Dunant and the Red Cross
abschnitte.text: After the Battle of Solferino in Italy in 1859, **Henry Dunant** from Geneva saw how thousands of wounded men were left without help. He worked to make sure that all the wounded would be helped, no matter which side they had fought on. In 1863 the **International Committee of the Red Cross** was founded in Geneva, and he was part of it. In 1901 Dunant received the first **Nobel Peace Prize**.

gewusst: The Red Cross emblem is the Swiss flag reversed: a red cross on a white background.
The Federal Constitution also protects the ‘dignity of living beings’, that is of animals and plants.

teile.einleitung: Artificial intelligence, or AI for short, writes texts, recognises faces and helps with decisions. The ethics of AI asks how such systems can be used fairly, safely and in the interests of people.
wichtigste: The EU's AI Act of 2024 sorts AI systems into levels of risk.
In the EU, social scoring is banned as an unacceptable risk.
Algorithmic bias often comes from distorted training data.
Explainable AI is meant to make machines' decisions understandable.
Deepfakes are AI forgeries that look deceptively real.
In 2024 the Council of Europe created the first binding international agreement on AI.
The alignment problem asks how AI can be tied to human values.

abschnitte.text: Long before today's computers, people were already thinking about moral machines. In 1942, in the short story ‘Runaround’, the writer **Isaac Asimov** formulated three **Laws of Robotics**. The first forbids a robot to injure a human being. These laws come from science fiction, but they are still quoted in debates about AI today.

AI systems learn from large amounts of data. If this data contains prejudices, the AI takes them on. This is called **algorithmic bias**, a systematic distortion. For example, some facial recognition systems were shown to recognise people with dark skin less well. That is why it is important to check data carefully and test systems for **fairness**.

Many learning systems are regarded as a **‘black box’**, because you cannot see how they reach a decision. That is tricky when it comes to loans, job applications or medicine. **Explainable AI**, XAI for short, is meant to make the reasons for a decision visible. Then people can check it and step in if there are mistakes.

**Deepfakes** are forgeries of videos, pictures or voices made with AI that look real. The name is made up of ‘deep learning’ and ‘fake’. They are a problem when used for disinformation, fraud or damaging someone's reputation. A big question for the future is the **alignment problem**: how can we make sure that an AI does what people really want? Even small mistakes in setting its goals can lead to unwanted behaviour.

In 2024 the EU adopted the **AI Act**. It distinguishes unacceptable, high, limited and minimal risk. The higher the risk, the stricter the obligations. Banned, for example, is **social scoring**, in which people get points for their behaviour and can be disadvantaged. Also in 2024 the **Council of Europe** adopted a framework convention on AI, human rights, democracy and the rule of law. Switzerland helped to draw it up.

gewusst: The Council of Europe's framework convention on AI is also open to states outside Europe.
During his life Isaac Asimov wrote or edited several hundred books.

teile.einleitung: Animal welfare means protecting animals from suffering, pain and poor living conditions. Switzerland has a strict law for this. Organisations, animal shelters and every individual can also do a lot for animals.
wichtigste: Switzerland's current Animal Welfare Act has applied since 2008.
The Federal Constitution includes the concept of the ‘dignity of living beings’.
Keeping animals appropriately means keeping them according to their needs.
In Switzerland guinea pigs must not be kept alone, because they are sociable.
World Animal Day is on 4 October.
The WWF was founded in 1961 in Morges on Lake Geneva.
Animals without a home often go to an animal shelter.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland's current **Animal Welfare Act** was passed by parliament in 2005 and has applied since **2008**. By international standards it is considered strict. It protects not only against pain and suffering but explicitly also the **dignity of the animal**. Since 1992 the Federal Constitution has used the term **‘dignity of living beings’** for this. An animal welfare ordinance sets out many details, for example how much space an animal needs.

Keeping animals **appropriately for their species** means keeping them in a way that suits their **needs**. They need enough space, exercise, things to do and suitable food. This is different for every species. **Guinea pigs**, for example, are **sociable animals**, so in Switzerland they must not be kept alone. This also applies to other social animals such as budgerigars or rabbits.

For **animal experiments**, the **3R principle** applies: **Replace**, **Reduce** and **Refine**. So animal experiments should be replaced by other methods wherever possible. Where this is not possible, fewer animals should be used and the strain on them should be reduced.

The **WWF** was founded in **1961** in **Morges** on Lake Geneva. Today its international headquarters are in Gland in the canton of Vaud, and its emblem is the **giant panda**. The WWF works mainly for nature and wild animals. Animals that no longer have a home often go to an **animal shelter**. There they are cared for until they find new owners. Many animal shelters are run by animal welfare societies.

**World Animal Day** is on **4 October**. On this day the Church also remembers **Saint Francis of Assisi**. He lived in Italy in the 13th century and is regarded as the **patron saint of animals**. According to legend, he even preached to the birds. He saw animals as the brothers and sisters of human beings.

gewusst: The first World Animal Day took place in Berlin in 1925; in 1931 it was declared an international day.
World Animal Day falls on the feast day of Saint Francis of Assisi.

teile.einleitung: In organ donation, a person gives an organ so that someone who is ill can go on living. Most organs come from people who have died. In Switzerland the Transplantation Act sets out exactly when and how donation is allowed.
wichtigste: On 15 May 2022 Swiss voters approved the extended opt-out solution.
The proposal received about 60 per cent of the vote.
Before that, the extended consent solution applied.
‘Extended’ means that the relatives are involved.
Before organs are removed, brain death must be confirmed.
Swisstransplant coordinates the allocation of organs.
Organ donations must be free of charge.

abschnitte.text: On **15 May 2022** the Swiss people voted on a change to the **Transplantation Act**. With **about 60 per cent** voting yes, the **extended opt-out solution** was approved. Under it, anyone who did not object during their lifetime counts as a donor. Before that the **extended consent solution** applied: organs could only be removed if the person or their relatives had agreed. The new rule needs a register, which is why putting it into practice takes several years.

The word **‘extended’** means that the **relatives** are involved. If there is no documented decision, they are asked. They can refuse a removal if they know or suspect that the person would have been against it. That is why it helps to talk about the subject with your family. People in society judge the question differently, and every decision must be respected.

Before organs may be removed from a person who has died, **brain death** must be confirmed. This means that all functions of the brain have permanently stopped. Two specialists must confirm this independently of each other. Donation must be **free of charge**: nobody may receive money or other advantages for it. Trading in organs is a criminal offence.

The national foundation **Swisstransplant** coordinates the **allocation** of donor organs on behalf of the federal government and keeps the waiting list. Who receives an organ is decided according to legal criteria, for example medical urgency and waiting time. This is meant to make the distribution fair. Many people on the waiting list urgently need an organ.

In **April 1969** the surgeon **Åke Senning** carried out Switzerland's first heart transplant in **Zurich**. The world's first heart transplant had taken place in Cape Town in 1967. Living people can also donate. The most common is donating a **kidney**, because you can live well with one healthy kidney. It is also possible to donate part of the liver.

gewusst: Åke Senning came from Sweden and had earlier fitted the first pacemaker to be implanted in a human being.
After a partial donation, the liver can grow back.

teile.einleitung: Medical ethics asks what is right and good in medicine. It deals with questions such as: who decides about a treatment? How can scarce resources be shared out fairly? What rules apply to research on human beings?
wichtigste: Beauchamp and Childress name four principles: autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence and justice.
A treatment needs the informed consent of the patient.
Paternalism means deciding against a person's will for their supposed good.
The Nuremberg Code of 1947 laid down rules for experiments on humans.
The World Medical Association adopted the Declaration of Geneva in 1948 and the Declaration of Helsinki in 1964.
Triage is sorting people by urgency when resources are not enough for everyone.
In Switzerland the advance directive has been regulated in the Civil Code since 2013.

abschnitte.text: In 1979 the Americans **Tom Beauchamp** and **James Childress** set out four principles that are widely used in everyday hospital life. **Autonomy** means respect for self-determination. **Non-maleficence** means not harming patients. **Beneficence** requires promoting their well-being, and **justice** a fair distribution. These principles can contradict each other and then have to be weighed against each other.

Before a treatment, **informed consent** is needed. The person must be given understandable information, be capable of judgement and be able to decide freely. Without consent, a medical procedure counts legally as bodily harm. The opposite is **paternalism**: experts decide against the will of a person who is capable of judgement, supposedly for their own good. The word comes from the Latin pater, father.

abschnitte.titel: Rules after the Second World War
abschnitte.text: Under the Nazis, doctors had carried out cruel experiments on people. In connection with the Nuremberg doctors' trial, the **Nuremberg Code** was drawn up in **1947**. Its first point requires the voluntary consent of the person being experimented on. In **1948** the **World Medical Association** adopted the **Declaration of Geneva**, a modern version of the Hippocratic Oath. In **1964** came the **Declaration of Helsinki**, with principles for medical research.

Sometimes there are not enough beds, machines or staff for everyone. Then patients are sorted according to urgency. This is called **triage**, from the French trier, to sort. Ethically this is very difficult, because human lives are at stake. That is why there are clear guidelines for it, so that decisions are not made arbitrarily.

The **Swiss Academy of Medical Sciences (SAMS)** draws up medical-ethical guidelines, for example on capacity for judgement or the end of life. The doctors' association **FMH** adopts many of them into its professional code, and they then become binding for its members. Since **1 January 2013** the **advance directive** has been expressly regulated in the Civil Code. With it, a person who is capable of judgement can decide in advance which treatments they agree to.

gewusst: The Hippocratic Oath is named after the Greek doctor Hippocrates, who lived about 2400 years ago.
The Declaration of Geneva has been revised several times, most recently in 2017.

teile.einleitung: Virtue ethics does not first ask ‘What should I do?’, but ‘What kind of person do I want to be?’. It goes back mainly to the Greek philosopher Aristotle. At its centre are good qualities of character, the virtues.
wichtigste: Aristotle's most important work on ethics is the ‘Nicomachean Ethics’.
According to Aristotle, every person strives for eudaimonia, the flourishing life.
The doctrine of the mean says: virtue is the middle between two extremes.
Courage lies between cowardice and foolhardiness.
Virtues of character are acquired through habit and practice.
Practical wisdom (phronesis) helps you decide correctly in concrete situations.
The four cardinal virtues are prudence, justice, courage and temperance.

abschnitte.text: **Aristotle** (384 to 322 BC) was a Greek philosopher and a pupil of Plato. He was also the teacher of the young Alexander the Great. His most important work on ethics is the **‘Nicomachean Ethics’**. It is probably named after his son or his father, who were both called Nicomachus. In it he asks how a person can live well.

According to Aristotle, every person ultimately strives for **eudaimonia**. The Greek word means a **flourishing life** or happiness. Everything else, such as money or fame, we only want because it contributes to this goal. Eudaimonia is not reached by chance but by living **virtuously**. What is meant is a life in which you develop your abilities well.

The **doctrine of the mean** says: a virtue is the **middle between two extremes**. **Courage** lies between **cowardice** and **foolhardiness**. Generosity lies between meanness and extravagance. But the right mean is not always exactly in the middle; it depends on the situation. To find it, you need **phronesis**, practical **wisdom**.

The ethical virtues, also called **virtues of character**, are not inborn. You acquire them through **habit and practice**. Aristotle compared this to learning a craft: you become just by acting justly, and brave by acting bravely. Over time, good action becomes a settled attitude. That is why upbringing is so important for him.

Since ancient times four **cardinal virtues** have been known: **prudence**, **justice**, **courage** and **temperance**. Other virtues, such as humility, are not among these four. For a long time virtue ethics stayed rather in the background. With his book **‘After Virtue’** (1981), the philosopher **Alasdair MacIntyre** contributed greatly to its revival. Today, alongside the ethics of duty and utilitarianism, it is one of the major approaches in ethics.

gewusst: The word ‘cardinal virtue’ comes from the Latin cardo, door hinge: all other virtues turn on these.
Aristotle founded his own school in Athens, the Lyceum.

teile.einleitung: The categorical imperative is the most important principle in Immanuel Kant's ethics. It is meant to show how you can test whether an action is morally right using reason alone.
wichtigste: Kant formulated the categorical imperative in 1785 in the ‘Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals’.
The basic formula requires you to act only on maxims that could become a universal law.
A maxim is a personal principle of what you will.
The formula of humanity says: never treat people merely as a means, but always also as an end.
A hypothetical imperative only applies if you have a particular goal.
Kant lived and taught almost all his life in Königsberg.
Autonomy of the will means that the will gives itself the law through reason.

abschnitte.text: **Immanuel Kant** (1724 to 1804) was one of the most important philosophers of the **Enlightenment**. He lived and taught almost all his life in **Königsberg** in East Prussia, today's Kaliningrad. In 1785 his work **‘Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals’** appeared. In it he set out the categorical imperative in detail for the first time. Later he developed his ethics further in other books.

The best-known version is called the **formula of universal law**: ‘Act only according to that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.’ A **maxim** is a subjective principle, that is a personal rule by which you act. You check: could this rule apply to all people without cancelling itself out? If not, according to Kant the action is immoral.

Kant explains his idea with an example: someone needs money and promises to pay it back, although he knows he cannot. If everyone acted like this, **nobody would believe promises any more**. Promising would lose its meaning. So the maxim cannot be made universal, and that is why the action is wrong. What matters to Kant is not the consequences but the contradiction in the rule itself.

Another version is the **formula of humanity**. It requires you to treat every person never **merely as a means**, but always also as an **end**. So you must not simply use others to reach your own goals. Every human being has a **dignity** that must be respected. This idea has strongly shaped modern thinking about **human dignity** and human rights.

A **hypothetical imperative** only applies under a condition: ‘If you want to stay healthy, take exercise.’ A **categorical imperative**, by contrast, applies unconditionally, to everyone and always. For Kant a person is free when they do not simply follow their wishes but give themselves the law through reason. He calls this **autonomy of the will**. Autonomy literally means ‘giving oneself the law’.

gewusst: Kant is said to have hardly ever left Königsberg and its surroundings, even though he thought about the whole world.
Kant did not think the categorical imperative was the same as the Golden Rule and explicitly distinguished it from it.

teile.einleitung: Happiness is a feeling of deep contentment and joy. Philosophers, psychologists and even whole states ask what makes people happy and how happiness can be measured.
wichtigste: For Aristotle, eudaimonia, the flourishing life, was the highest goal.
Hedonism sees pleasure as the most important goal; one of its representatives was Epicurus.
In flow you are completely absorbed in an activity.
Serotonin is often called the ‘happiness hormone’.
Finland has topped the World Happiness Report since 2018 (as of 2025).
Bhutan measures its success by ‘Gross National Happiness’.
The International Day of Happiness is on 20 March.

abschnitte.text: The ancient Greeks were already thinking about happiness. **Aristotle** called the flourishing, happy life **eudaimonia**. He saw it as humanity's highest goal and believed it could be reached through a virtuous, reasonable life. **Hedonism**, from the Greek ‘hedone’ for pleasure and joy, on the other hand, puts pleasure at the centre. A well-known representative was **Epicurus**. However, he taught that moderate pleasures and peace of mind were more important than luxury.

In the brain, **messenger substances** are at work that influence our mood. **Serotonin** is often called the ‘happiness hormone’. **Dopamine** and **endorphins** are also called this in everyday language. A special feeling of happiness is **flow**. In flow you are completely absorbed in an activity and forget the time. The term was coined by the psychologist **Mihály Csíkszentmihályi**. Flow often arises when a task is neither too easy nor too hard.

The **World Happiness Report** compares how satisfied people are in many countries every year. Since 2018 **Finland** has been in first place without a break (as of 2025). Switzerland is usually among the top ten. The country of **Bhutan** in the Himalayas measures its success by **Gross National Happiness**. It puts people's well-being above pure economic growth, and this goal is even written into its constitution.

The **UN General Assembly** declared **20 March** the International Day of Happiness. It has been marked since 2013. The day is meant to remind us that happiness and well-being are important goals for all people. The idea came from Bhutan. Many schools and organisations use the day to think about contentment and togetherness.

Many cultures have **lucky charms**. A well-known example is the **four-leaf clover**. Clover normally has three leaves; a four-leaf one is rare and is therefore seen as a symbol of luck. At New Year in Switzerland people also give each other chimney sweeps, horseshoes or little lucky pigs. Whether they really bring luck is another question, but they make many people happy.

gewusst: In the World Happiness Report people are asked how satisfied they are with their lives on a scale from 0 to 10.
The chimney sweep is seen as a lucky charm because in the past a clean chimney protected the house from fire.

teile.einleitung: Feelings are what we sense inside ourselves: joy, sadness, anger, fear and much more. All people have feelings, and it helps to recognise them and deal with them well.
wichtigste: All feelings are allowed, including anger and sadness.
Laughing and jumping about are signs of joy.
Tears often show sadness.
Clenched fists and a red face often show anger.
Fear warns us of danger.
Empathy means sensing how someone else is feeling.

abschnitte.text: You can often see feelings on someone's face and body. A child who **laughs and jumps about** is happy. If someone has **tears** in their eyes and hangs their head, they are probably sad. **Clenched fists** and a red face are often signs of anger. If you recognise feelings, you understand others better. If you are not sure, you can simply ask.

**Anger** is a strong feeling. It shows that something is bothering you. When you are very angry, it helps to **breathe deeply**. That calms the body down. Some people count slowly to ten or go away for a moment. Afterwards it is easier to say what is bothering you without hurting anyone.

**Fear** is the feeling you have when you are afraid of something. It is useful, because it **warns us of danger**. For example, if you feel afraid at a steep spot, you take more care. But sometimes a fear is bigger than it needs to be. Then it is good to talk to someone about it.

When you have managed something difficult, for example finished painting a difficult picture, you feel **proud**. You feel **envy** when you want something that someone else has, or begrudge them it. Everyone knows this feeling sometimes. You can then think about what you are good at yourself. Or you can be happy for the other person.

**Empathy** means putting yourself in other people's shoes. You sense how someone else is feeling. Then you can help better, for example by comforting them or listening. **All feelings are allowed**, including anger and sadness. What matters is how you deal with them. If you talk about your feelings, you often feel a bit better already.

gewusst: Many facial expressions, such as smiling, are understood by people all over the world.
Even tiny babies show feelings such as joy or discomfort, long before they can talk.

teile.einleitung: Intergenerational justice asks what we owe to the people who will live after us. It is about the environment, the climate, government debt and pensions, that is about sharing burdens and opportunities fairly between young and old.
wichtigste: The Brundtland Report of 1987 coined the best-known definition of sustainability.
The intergenerational contract is an image for solidarity in pension provision.
The federal debt brake was approved by the people in 2001.
In 2024 the KlimaSeniorinnen (Senior Women for Climate Protection) won against Switzerland in Strasbourg.
Discounting gives future costs less weight than present ones.
On 3 March 2024 voters approved a 13th AVS pension payment.
Since 2015 Wales has had a Commissioner for Future Generations.

abschnitte.text: In 1987 the UN report **‘Our Common Future’** was published, led by the Norwegian **Gro Harlem Brundtland**. It is called the **Brundtland Report**. It coined the best-known definition of sustainable development: meeting the needs of the present without taking away the ability of future generations to meet theirs. This made consideration for coming generations a political goal.

The **intergenerational contract** is not a real contract. It is an image for the fact that the younger generation pays for the pensions of the older one and will later be provided for itself. On 3 March 2024 Swiss voters approved the **initiative for a 13th AVS pension payment** by about 58 per cent. The pension initiative to raise the retirement age was clearly rejected on the same day. The debate was very much about how the burden is shared between young and old.

Taking on debts today puts a burden on the future. That is why in 2001 Swiss voters approved the **debt brake** with about 85 per cent voting yes. It has been applied since 2003. Over a whole economic cycle, federal spending should not exceed income. An **economic cycle** is the ups and downs of the economy over several years.

On 9 April 2024 the **European Court of Human Rights** in Strasbourg ruled on a complaint by the association **KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz**. It found that Switzerland had violated the right to respect for private and family life because it was doing too little against climate change. The judgment is often discussed in connection with duties towards coming generations. Opinions about it are divided in Switzerland.

In economic calculations, future costs and benefits are often **given less weight** than present ones. This method is called **discounting**. The higher the discount rate, the less future climate damage counts today. That is why choosing the rate is also an ethical question. Some countries create special offices for the future: since 2015 **Wales** has had a law obliging public bodies to consider long-term consequences, and it has a Commissioner for Future Generations.

gewusst: Gro Harlem Brundtland was the first woman to become Prime Minister of Norway.
The KlimaSeniorinnen are an association of older women who see themselves as particularly affected by heatwaves.

teile.einleitung: Someone who is helpful helps others when they need support. It can be something small, like carrying bags, or something important, like getting help after an accident.
wichtigste: Helpfulness means helping others when they need it.
If a child is crying because they have fallen over, you go over and help.
Before you help, it is best to ask whether the help is wanted.
In Switzerland you reach the ambulance on 144 and the fire brigade on 118.
Children and teenagers with worries can call the number 147.
You can help at home too, for example by laying the table.
Anyone who has been helped says ‘thank you’.

abschnitte.titel: Small acts of help every day
abschnitte.text: Helpfulness begins with small things. If a child has fallen over and is crying, you go over, comfort them and fetch an adult if necessary. If an older man is carrying heavy bags up the stairs, you ask kindly whether you can help. Asking is important, because not everyone wants help. In this way you show **consideration** and **respect**.

A family works better if everyone helps. You can **lay the table**, clear it, tidy your room or help carry the shopping. Helping little brothers and sisters get dressed is also helpful. If you help, you learn responsibility and take some of the load off the others.

After a serious accident you get help straight away. In Switzerland you call the **ambulance** on **144**, the **fire brigade** on **118** and the **police** on **117**. The European emergency number **112** also works. On the phone you say calmly who you are, where you are and what has happened. That is important help too, even if you cannot do anything else yourself.

Children and teenagers who have worries can call the number **147**. There, trained people listen and help, free of charge and in confidence. The number belongs to the foundation **Pro Juventute**. You can also call if you are worried about a friend. Getting help is brave and right.

Anyone who receives help says **‘thank you’**. This shows that you value the help. Helpfulness not only makes others happy, but often you too. Many people in Switzerland even help in their free time, for example in clubs or the fire brigade. This unpaid work is called **volunteering**.

gewusst: In many Swiss municipalities the fire brigade is made up largely of volunteers who help alongside their jobs.
You can not only call the number 147, you can also get in touch by chat or message.

teile.einleitung: Justice means that people are treated fairly and each person gets what they are entitled to. People have been thinking about what exactly is just since ancient times.
wichtigste: Justitia, the figure of justice, carries scales and a sword.
The blindfold stands for judging without regard to who someone is.
In justice according to need, everyone gets what they need.
Equality of opportunity means the same possibilities for everyone.
Aristotle distinguished between distributive and corrective justice.
John Rawls invented the ‘veil of ignorance’.
The Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne is Switzerland's highest court.

abschnitte.text: Justice is often shown as a woman, **Justitia** (Lady Justice). In her hands she holds **scales** and a **sword**. The scales stand for careful weighing up, the sword for enforcing the law. She often wears a **blindfold**. It shows that the law applies equally to everyone, without regard to who they are. In Bern there is the **Gerechtigkeitsbrunnen** (Fountain of Justice) with such a figure.

A simple form of justice is **equal distribution**. If three children share 12 biscuits equally, each gets 4 biscuits. But equal is not always just. In **justice according to need**, those who need more get more, for example a child who is ill gets more help. In **justice according to merit**, you receive according to what you have achieved.

**Equality of opportunity** means that everyone should have the same starting conditions, for example in access to education. What you make of them is then up to you. In 1971, in ‘A Theory of Justice’, the philosopher **John Rawls** described the **veil of ignorance**. You should choose rules without knowing what place you yourself will have in society. This produces rules that are fair for everyone.

The Greek philosopher **Aristotle** was already thinking about justice. In the ‘Nicomachean Ethics’ he distinguished two kinds. **Distributive justice** concerns how goods and honours are shared out in a community. **Corrective justice** concerns, for example, fair exchanges or compensation for damage. This distinction is still used today.

To make sure the law is applied fairly, there are **courts**. In Switzerland the cantonal courts give judgment first. The country's highest court is the **Federal Supreme Court**. Its main seat is in **Lausanne**, and as the last instance it reviews judgments of the cantonal courts. Independent courts are an important part of the **rule of law**.

gewusst: The Fountain of Justice in Bern dates from the 16th century.
Besides Lausanne, the Federal Supreme Court also has a site in Lucerne.

teile.einleitung: Children's rights are special rights for everyone under 18. They are set out in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and are meant to protect children, help them develop and give them a voice.
wichtigste: The UN adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child on 20 November 1989.
Every person under 18 counts as a child.
Switzerland joined the Convention in 1997.
The well-being of the child must come first in all decisions.
Article 12 guarantees the right to be heard.
Children's rights also include education, play and leisure.
The USA is the only UN member that has not ratified the Convention (as of 2025).

abschnitte.titel: The Convention on the Rights of the Child
abschnitte.text: The **UN General Assembly** adopted the **Convention on the Rights of the Child** on **20 November 1989**. That is why 20 November is the international day of children's rights. According to Article 1, every person **under 18** counts as a child. Almost every country in the world has ratified the Convention, that is accepted it as binding. Only the **USA** has signed it but never ratified it (as of 2025).

**Switzerland** ratified the Convention in **1997**. Since then it has had to report regularly to the UN on how it is putting children's rights into practice. A committee of experts examines these reports and makes recommendations. There was a link with Switzerland even earlier: in 1924 the League of Nations in **Geneva** adopted a first declaration on the rights of the child.

Article 3 requires that the **best interests of the child** be a primary consideration in all measures. This applies to courts, authorities and schools. According to Article 12, children have the **right to be heard**: they may give their opinion on everything that affects them. This opinion must be taken into account according to their age and maturity. In addition, children must not be disadvantaged, no matter where they come from.

Every child has a **right to education**. If children have to work in factories instead of going to school, this right is violated. The Convention also protects children from economic exploitation and violence. Article 31 guarantees the **right to play and leisure**, to rest and to cultural activities. Playing is important for healthy development.

The UN's children's fund is called **UNICEF**. It was founded in **1946** and works for children's rights all over the world. UNICEF helps with health, clean water, education and protection, especially in poor countries and in disasters. In Switzerland other organisations also work for children's rights, for example Pro Juventute with its helpline number 147.

gewusst: The Convention on the Rights of the Child is the human rights treaty that more countries around the world have joined than any other.
The Convention has 54 articles and applies to every child, whatever their language, religion or origin.

teile.einleitung: Rules say what is allowed and what is not. They help people to live together well and safely. There are rules at school, on the roads, in games and throughout the country.
wichtigste: Rules exist so that everyone can live together well.
As a pedestrian you may cross the road when the light is green.
At zebra crossings in Switzerland the rule is: ‘Warte, luege, lose, laufe’.
If you want to say something in class, you put up your hand.
A class can agree rules together with the teacher.
A cycle helmet protects your head when cycling.
Rules that apply to everyone in a country are called laws.

abschnitte.text: At school there are rules so that **everyone can get on well** and learn. If you want to say something, you **put up your hand**, so that not everyone talks at once. Often the **class** agrees rules together with the **teacher**. Rules like these are easier to understand, and people are happier to keep to them. In the playground, the usual rule for ball games is: do not hit anyone with the ball on purpose.

On the **roads**, rules protect people from accidents. As a pedestrian you cross the road when the light is **green** and wait when it is red. Before crossing at a zebra crossing, children in Switzerland learn: **‘Warte, luege, lose, laufe’**. In Swiss German this means: stop, look left and right, listen, and only then walk. When **cycling** it is best to wear a **cycle helmet**; it protects your head if you fall.

Every game has **rules**. They make sure that the game is fair and that everyone has the same chances. If nobody keeps to the rules, there is often a **quarrel**. You can also change the rules together if everyone agrees. The only important thing is to agree before the game starts.

Rules that apply to everyone in a country are called **laws**. In Switzerland **parliament** decides on federal laws. But the people can have a say: with a **referendum** they can vote on a law. The **cantons** and **municipalities** also have their own rules. Anyone who does not keep to the law can expect a penalty.

gewusst: The saying ‘Warte, luege, lose, laufe’ is Swiss German and is already practised in kindergarten.
In Switzerland the people can vote directly on many laws, which is rare in the world.

teile.einleitung: An ethical dilemma is a predicament: you have to choose between two options, and each one breaks an important duty. Philosophy, psychology and law use such dilemmas to think about morality.
wichtigste: In a real dilemma, two duties rule each other out.
Lawrence Kohlberg used the Heinz dilemma to study moral development.
The highest level in Kohlberg's scheme is the post-conventional level.
The plank of Carneades is an ancient thought experiment.
The tragedy of the commons describes the overuse of shared resources.
In the prisoner's dilemma, self-interest leads both into a worse outcome.
The principle of double effect goes back to Thomas Aquinas.

abschnitte.text: In a **moral dilemma** there are two well-founded duties, but you can only fulfil one. Whoever chooses one inevitably breaks the other. So there is **no way out without a moral loss**. A very old example is the **plank of Carneades**: two shipwrecked men fight over a plank that can only carry one. The Greek philosopher Carneades asked whether you may push the other one away. In law this is regarded as an example of excusable necessity.

The psychologist **Lawrence Kohlberg** presented people with the **Heinz dilemma**. In it, a man wonders whether he should steal an unaffordable medicine for his terminally ill wife. Kohlberg was not interested in the answer but in the **reasoning**. From this he developed stages of moral development. At the highest, the **post-conventional level**, people are guided by general principles such as justice, even against the rules in force.

In 1968, in the journal ‘Science’, **Garrett Hardin** described the **tragedy of the commons**. If everyone takes their own advantage from a shared pasture, it is destroyed for everyone. The economist **Elinor Ostrom** later showed that communities such as Swiss **alpine pasture cooperatives** can prevent this with clever rules. Similarly, the **prisoner's dilemma** from game theory shows: betrayal pays off for each person individually, but staying silent together would be better.

In 2006 Germany's Federal Constitutional Court ruled on shooting down a hijacked passenger plane with innocent people on board. It declared the rule in the Aviation Security Act **unconstitutional**. The state must not sacrifice innocent people as mere objects, and human lives must **not be weighed against each other**. Questions like these show how hard dilemmas are in real life.

The **principle of double effect** goes back to **Thomas Aquinas**. Under certain conditions it allows a good action even if a terrible side effect can be foreseen. But the terrible effect must not be intended and must not be the means to the end. Garrett Hardin's **lifeboat ethics** of 1974 is controversial. He compared rich countries to a lifeboat that sinks if it is overloaded and rejected unlimited aid. His position was strongly criticised.

gewusst: In 2009 Elinor Ostrom became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Economics.
Garrett Hardin deliberately set his lifeboat ethics against the image of ‘spaceship Earth’.

teile.einleitung: The trolley problem is one of the best-known thought experiments in ethics. It asks whether you may cause harm in order to prevent greater harm. Today it also plays a part in the debate about self-driving cars.
wichtigste: The British philosopher Philippa Foot formulated the problem in 1967.
In 1976 Judith Jarvis Thomson coined the name ‘trolley problem’.
In the basic version, a utilitarian would switch the points.
The doctrine of double effect distinguishes intended consequences from those that are accepted.
Many people find pushing a man off a bridge more wrong, because he is used as a means.
With the ‘Moral Machine’, MIT collected millions of judgements about autonomous vehicles.
German guidelines from 2017 forbid choosing victims by age or other characteristics.

abschnitte.text: A tram, in American English a **trolley**, is rolling out of control towards five people. You could switch the **points**, and then it would go onto another track where one person is standing. Should you switch them? The British philosopher **Philippa Foot** formulated the example in an essay in **1967**. It is an imaginary situation meant to help people think about moral principles.

In **1976** the American **Judith Jarvis Thomson** coined the name **‘trolley problem’** and invented further versions. In the **bridge version**, you could only stop the tram by pushing a man off a bridge onto the tracks. Many people find this much worse than switching the points, even though the result would be the same. One reason: the man would be used as a **mere means**. With the points, the death is a side effect.

For **utilitarianism**, the consequences count: one victim is less bad than five, so a utilitarian would **switch the points**. Other approaches stress that people must not be used as a means, as Kant demanded. The **doctrine of double effect**, which goes back to **Thomas Aquinas**, distinguishes between **intended** consequences and those that are only **accepted**. Philosophers use it to try to explain why the two versions feel so different.

Today the question arises in a new form: how should an **autonomous vehicle** decide in an unavoidable accident? With the online experiment **‘Moral Machine’**, **MIT** in the USA collected millions of judgements from all over the world. The results were published in the journal ‘Nature’ in 2018 and showed differences between regions of the world. In **2017** a German **ethics commission** laid down that victims must not be chosen according to **personal characteristics such as age**.

Courts have also had to rule on similar questions. A German law allowed a hijacked passenger plane to be shot down in order to save other people. In **2006** the **Federal Constitutional Court** declared this rule **incompatible with human dignity** and void. The passengers must not be treated as mere objects for saving others.

gewusst: Philippa Foot was originally not interested in trams at all, but in the doctrine of double effect.
The trolley problem is one of the most discussed examples in ethics and is often talked about in schools and universities.

teile.einleitung: A generation is a group of people who were born at roughly the same time. A family often includes three or four generations: children, parents, grandparents and sometimes great-grandparents.
wichtigste: In the **intergenerational contract**, people in work pay the pensions of older people.
Switzerland has had the AVS (old-age insurance) since 1948.
The baby boomers are the large age groups born after the Second World War.
Generation Z was born roughly between 1997 and 2012.
Pro Senectute has been working for older people since 1917.
The International Day of Older Persons is on 1 October.

abschnitte.text: A **generation** includes people who were born at roughly the same time and have had similar experiences. The large age groups born after the Second World War are called **baby boomers**. After 1945 a great many children were born in many countries. **Generation Z** was born roughly between 1997 and 2012. It grew up with smartphones and the internet. After that comes **Generation Alpha**.

The **Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance (AVS)** is the most important pillar of Swiss pension provision. The people approved it in 1947, and the first pensions were paid out in 1948. The AVS works on the **pay-as-you-go system**. People in work pay today's pensions with their contributions. Later they receive pensions themselves from the younger generation. This principle is called the **intergenerational contract**.

The Swiss foundation **Pro Senectute** has been working for older people since 1917. The name is Latin and means ‘for old age’. It offers advice, courses and support for older people. Since 1991 the UN has marked the International Day of Older Persons every year on **1 October**. It honours the achievements of older people.

In a **multi-generation house**, young and old deliberately live together and help each other. Older people look after children, for example, and younger people help with shopping or with the computer. In this way all generations benefit. Grandparents who look after their grandchildren are another example of generations being there for each other.

Each generation grows up in different conditions. This can lead to differences of opinion, for example about fashion, music or technology. This is called a **generation gap** or conflict between generations. If people listen to each other, they can learn a lot from each other. The younger ones often know new technology, while the older ones have a lot of life experience.

gewusst: The 1947 vote on the AVS was approved by a large majority.
The word ‘senior’ comes from the Latin ‘senex’, old.

teile.einleitung: Volunteering is work that people do unpaid for others or for the community. In Switzerland many people volunteer, in clubs, in their neighbourhood or in public offices.
wichtigste: An unpaid post, for example on a club committee, is called an **honorary position**.
In the **militia system**, citizens hold public offices alongside their jobs.
The **Sozialzeitausweis** (volunteering certificate) confirms voluntary work.
Jubla and the Scouts are largely run by young volunteers.
International Volunteer Day is on 5 December.
Helping your neighbours also counts as informal volunteering.

abschnitte.text: There are two kinds of volunteering. **Formal volunteering** takes place in organisations, for example in sports clubs, churches or charities. **Informal volunteering** happens outside clubs, for example when you help your neighbour with her shopping. An unpaid post, for example on a club's committee, is called an **honorary position**. People in honorary positions receive no wages, at most a small allowance.

In Switzerland many municipal councillors, firefighters and members of parliament work **part-time alongside their jobs**. This system is called the **militia system**. It depends on citizens taking on public tasks as well as their jobs. As a result, those in charge know people's everyday lives well. At the same time, some municipalities today find it hard to find enough people for their offices.

In the **Scouts**, older teenagers lead the groups of younger ones as volunteers. Their sign is the neckerchief. The Scout movement was founded by the Briton **Robert Baden-Powell**. In **Jubla**, the association of Jungwacht and Blauring, young adults lead group sessions and camps for children. Jubla has a church background. In both organisations, young leaders learn to take responsibility.

Many organisations could not exist without volunteers. **Tischlein deck dich** saves surplus food from being thrown away. Volunteers hand it out to people affected by poverty in Switzerland. Volunteers also lend a hand with visiting services, lunch clubs and homework help. This creates support that the state could not provide on its own.

With the **Sozialzeitausweis**, volunteers can have their work, tasks and hours officially confirmed. This helps, for example, with job applications, because the commitment becomes visible. In 1985 the UN declared **5 December** International Volunteer Day. On this day people all over the world thank everyone who works for others without pay.

gewusst: The word ‘militia’ comes from the Latin ‘militia’, military service, and originally meant citizens who did military service alongside their jobs.
Many Swiss municipalities are run by a part-time municipal council.

teile.einleitung: ‘A Theory of Justice’ is the main work of the American philosopher John Rawls. The book appeared in 1971 and asks according to which principles a just society should be built.
wichtigste: John Rawls published ‘A Theory of Justice’ in 1971.
He sums up his theory as ‘justice as fairness’.
In the **original position**, free and equal people choose the principles of justice.
Behind the **veil of ignorance** nobody knows their future position.
Equal basic liberties for all have priority.
The difference principle only allows inequality if it benefits the least well-off most.
In 1974 Robert Nozick criticised Rawls from a libertarian point of view.

abschnitte.text: **John Rawls** lived from 1921 to 2002 and taught at Harvard University. His book **‘A Theory of Justice’** appeared in 1971 and greatly revived political philosophy. In German it is called ‘Eine Theorie der Gerechtigkeit’. Rawls sums up his theory with the slogan **‘justice as fairness’**. He deliberately sets it against **utilitarianism**, which only looks at the greatest total benefit.

Rawls carries out a thought experiment. In the **original position**, people are to choose the rules of their society. They are free, equal and rational. But they are behind a **veil of ignorance**: nobody knows their background, talents, wealth or future position. So nobody chooses rules that favour only themselves. The principles are fair because they are chosen under fair conditions.

The **first principle** guarantees everyone an equal system of **basic liberties**, such as freedom of opinion and freedom of conscience. This principle has **priority** over all others. Basic liberties must not be restricted just to gain economic advantages. The second principle also demands **fair equality of opportunity** in access to offices and positions.

According to the **difference principle**, inequalities in income and wealth are only allowed if they benefit the **least advantaged** the most. So a doctor may earn more if this benefits everyone, including the poorest. Why choose this way? According to Rawls, in the original position people use the **maximin rule**: you choose the option whose worst outcome is the best. If you do not know where you will end up, you protect yourself against the worst fate.

Rawls's theory was widely discussed. **Robert Nozick**, a colleague at Harvard University, criticised it in 1974 in ‘Anarchy, State, and Utopia’ from a **libertarian** point of view. He defended a minimal state and saw redistribution through taxes as an intrusion into property rights. Others thought that Rawls demanded too little equality. To this day the book is a basic text of political philosophy.

gewusst: As a young soldier, John Rawls served in the Pacific in the Second World War.
‘A Theory of Justice’ has been translated into many languages.

teile.einleitung: Utilitarianism is a school of thought in ethics. It asks: which action brings the most happiness and the least suffering overall? This idea still shapes many discussions about politics, the economy and animal welfare today.
wichtigste: The Englishman Jeremy Bentham (1748 to 1832) is regarded as the founder of classical utilitarianism.
The aim is: the greatest happiness of the greatest number.
Utilitarianism judges actions by their consequences and therefore belongs to consequentialism.
John Stuart Mill distinguished higher, intellectual pleasures from lower, bodily ones.
Rule utilitarianism judges rules, act utilitarianism individual actions.
Peter Singer demands that the interests of all beings capable of suffering be considered equally.
Critics warn that the rights of individuals could be sacrificed to the overall benefit.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin ‘utilitas’, which means usefulness. According to utilitarianism, the right action is the one that produces the most **well-being** overall. The happiness of each person affected counts equally, whether rich or poor. The famous formula is: **the greatest happiness of the greatest number**. So you do not look at the intention but at what comes out in the end. That is why utilitarianism belongs to **consequentialism**, the ethics of consequences.

The English philosopher **Jeremy Bentham** made the principle of utility the basis of morality and law-making. His main work appeared in 1789. Bentham wanted to make pleasure and pain measurable. With the **hedonic calculus** you were supposed to weigh up pleasure and pain according to criteria such as intensity, duration, certainty and nearness. In this way he wanted to solve the question of the best action almost like a maths problem.

abschnitte.titel: John Stuart Mill and the quality of pleasure
abschnitte.text: In the 19th century **John Stuart Mill** developed Bentham's ideas further. For him it mattered not only how much pleasure is produced, but also what kind of pleasure. He distinguished **higher**, intellectual pleasures, such as reading or learning, from **lower**, bodily pleasures. He is the source of the sentence: ‘It is better to be a dissatisfied human being than a satisfied pig.’

There are different forms of utilitarianism. **Act utilitarianism** examines each individual action on its own. **Rule utilitarianism**, on the other hand, asks which generally followed rule would have the best consequences. This can be used, for example, to justify the rule ‘keep your promises’, even if breaking one would be useful in a particular case. Because if nobody keeps promises any more, everyone loses trust.

Bentham thought that with animals what matters is not whether they can think or speak, but whether they can **suffer**. The Australian **Peter Singer** holds a form of preference utilitarianism and in 1975 wrote the book ‘Animal Liberation’. He criticises favouring one's own species as **speciesism**. A common objection to utilitarianism is that it could sacrifice the rights of individuals if many people benefit. Critics see this as a problem for justice and human dignity.

gewusst: Jeremy Bentham had his body preserved after his death. His clothed skeleton with a wax head still sits in a cabinet at University College London today.
When experts in politics compare the costs and benefits of a measure, there is often a utilitarian idea behind it.

teile.einleitung: Respect means valuing other people, animals, nature and other people's things. Respectful people are considerate and treat others kindly. Respect is important for living well together.
wichtigste: If you let others finish speaking, you show respect.
In Switzerland people often greet each other with ‘Grüezi’.
You treat other people's things carefully.
Taking your rubbish home shows respect for nature.
If someone does not want to be hugged, you respect that.
On the bus you offer your seat to older people.
A swear word is an insulting word.

abschnitte.text: You show respect in conversation: you let others **finish speaking** and you listen. You greet each other in a friendly way, in German-speaking Switzerland often with **‘Grüezi’**. On the **bus** you offer your seat to older people. **Swear words** are insulting words and hurt others. Respectful people do without them, even when they are angry.

Every person may decide for themselves who is allowed to touch them. If a child does **not want to be hugged**, then you do not hug them. This also applies among friends and in the family. A ‘no’ must be taken seriously. That shows respect for the other person's wishes.

You treat other people's things **carefully**. You give back a borrowed book in good condition, and you only use someone else's bicycle if you have asked. This also includes school materials and public things such as playgrounds or benches. If you break something, you say so honestly. That way things stay usable for everyone.

**Nature** deserves respect too. You **take** your **rubbish home** instead of leaving it lying around, and you do not pick protected plants. You leave **animals** in peace, especially wild animals in the forest. You do not chase them and do not simply feed them. That way their habitats stay protected.

Switzerland has four national languages. As well as **‘Grüezi’** you hear **‘Bonjour’** in French, **‘Buongiorno’** in Italian and **‘Allegra’** in Romansh. Respect also means valuing other languages, customs and opinions. The word respect comes from the Latin respectus, which means roughly ‘consideration’.

gewusst: In Switzerland many people say ‘Grüezi’ even to strangers when they are out hiking.
In Romansh, ‘Allegra’ originally means ‘be glad’.

teile.einleitung: Friendship is a special bond between people who like each other and trust each other. Good friends stick together, listen and have fun together.
wichtigste: Good friends stick together, even when things are difficult.
If you listen and ask questions, you show that the other person matters to you.
You can have lots of friends.
You keep harmless secrets to yourself.
If a secret means that someone is being hurt, you get help.
A compliment is something nice you say about someone.

abschnitte.text: Good friends **stick together**. They support each other, even when things are difficult. They spend **time together**, playing, talking and laughing. That makes the friendship stronger. You can be friends with more than one child. Every friendship is something special.

When a friend is sad, you can **ask what is wrong**. Often it helps just to **listen**. If a friend has made a mistake in a drawing, you can say: ‘That can happen to anyone.’ Encouraging words are comforting. A **compliment** is a friendly remark, for example ‘You've drawn that beautifully’. It makes others happy.

A new child in the class often does not know anyone yet and feels unsure. It is friendly to **invite the child to play**. That makes it easier for them to fit in. Many friendships begin with a small invitation or a smile. If you are open towards others, you often find new friends yourself.

If a friend tells you a secret that does not harm anyone, you keep it **to yourself**. That shows that people can **trust** you. But there are secrets where someone is afraid or is being hurt. You may and should tell such secrets to an **adult you trust**, for example your parents or a teacher. That is not betrayal but help.

On the internet and in the class chat there are also rules for treating each other well. They are called **netiquette**. The word is made up of ‘net’ and ‘etiquette’. This includes staying friendly and **not showing others up**. What you would not say to someone's face, you do not write in the chat either.

gewusst: The UN's International Day of Friendship is on 30 July.
Friendships also exist between people of different ages, for example between children and grandparents.

teile.einleitung: Environmental ethics asks what responsibility humans have towards nature. Do only humans have moral value, or do animals, plants and whole ecosystems have it too? There are different positions and important principles on this.
wichtigste: According to anthropocentrism, only humans have intrinsic moral value.
Pathocentrism grants intrinsic value to all living things that can suffer.
Albert Schweitzer coined the phrase ‘reverence for life’.
In 1949 Aldo Leopold formulated the ‘land ethic’.
In 1973 Arne Naess coined the term ‘deep ecology’.
In 1713 Hans Carl von Carlowitz applied the idea of sustainability to forests.
The polluter pays principle and the precautionary principle are important principles of environmental protection.

abschnitte.text: Environmental ethics distinguishes several positions. According to **anthropocentrism**, only **humans** have intrinsic moral value, and nature matters because it is useful to people. **Pathocentrism** grants intrinsic value to all living things that are **able to suffer**. **Biocentrism** includes all living things, including plants. Finally, **holism** takes whole ecosystems into account.

The doctor and theologian **Albert Schweitzer** coined the phrase **‘reverence for life’**. For him all life deserves respect, not only human life. This attitude is seen as the basis of a **biocentric** ethics. Schweitzer founded a hospital in Lambaréné in what is now Gabon and received the Nobel Peace Prize. His ideas influenced many later environmentalists.

In his book **‘A Sand County Almanac’** (1949), the American **Aldo Leopold** formulated the **‘land ethic’**. According to it, people should respect soils, waters, plants and animals as a community to which they themselves belong. In **1973** the Norwegian philosopher **Arne Naess** coined the term **deep ecology**. He demanded that nature be protected not only for the benefit of people but for its own sake.

The idea of **sustainability** originally comes from **forestry**. In **1713** the Saxon official **Hans Carl von Carlowitz** wrote that you should only cut as much wood as can grow back. Today sustainability means living in such a way that future generations will also have good living conditions. In Switzerland the Federal Constitution requires the federal government and the cantons to promote sustainable development. The Swiss Forest Act has long protected the area of forest.

According to the **polluter pays principle**, those who cause environmental pollution bear its costs. The **precautionary principle** demands that possible environmental damage be prevented even when there is still scientific **uncertainty**. So you do not wait until damage has definitely been proven. Both principles are laid down in the Swiss **Environmental Protection Act**. They also apply in many other countries and in international environmental law.

gewusst: The word ‘sustainable’ (in German ‘nachhaltig’) was first used for forests more than 300 years ago and is now on everyone's lips.
In 1979, in ‘The Imperative of Responsibility’, the philosopher Hans Jonas called for people to think about the consequences of their actions for future generations too.

teile.einleitung: Hope is the expectation that something good will happen. It gives people the strength to keep going, even in hard times. It plays a big part in religion, legends, history and language.
wichtigste: Hope means trusting in something good that is still to come.
Green is traditionally the colour of hope.
In Christianity the anchor is a symbol of hope.
Paul names faith, love and hope together.
In the legend of Pandora, hope stayed behind in the box.
Martin Luther King's words ‘I have a dream’ became a symbol of hope in 1963.
Resilience is the ability to regain strength after a crisis.

abschnitte.text: The colour **green** is traditionally seen as the colour of hope, because it reminds people of plants growing in spring. In Christianity the **anchor** is a symbol of hope: just as an anchor holds a ship steady in a storm, hope is meant to give people something to hold on to. In a letter, the apostle **Paul** names **faith, love and hope** together. They are called the three theological virtues.

A Greek legend tells of **Pandora**. She opened a jar from which all evils escaped into the world, such as illness and hardship. Only **hope** stayed behind inside. The legend is interpreted in different ways: some see hope as a comfort that remains for people. Today we say ‘to open Pandora's box’ when something sets off lots of problems.

The **Cape of Good Hope** is at the southern tip of Africa. The Portuguese seafarer Bartolomeu Dias sailed round it in 1488. The name expressed the hope of finding the sea route to India this way. In 1963 **Martin Luther King** gave a famous speech in Washington against the unfair treatment of Black people. His words **‘I have a dream’** became a symbol of the hope for equal rights.

Anyone who expects good things has an attitude of **optimism**. Hope can help you get through difficulties. The ability to regain strength after a crisis is called **resilience**. It comes from the Latin word for ‘to spring back’. Resilience can be strengthened, for example through good friendships and through people you trust.

The German saying **‘Die Hoffnung stirbt zuletzt’** (hope dies last) means that you should not give up too quickly. But hope is not the same as simply wishing: often it also means doing something yourself. The German philosopher **Ernst Bloch** wrote a large work called ‘The Principle of Hope’. In it he describes how people keep dreaming of a better future.

gewusst: Bartolomeu Dias is said to have first called the cape the ‘Cape of Storms’; only later did it get its hopeful name.
In the original Greek legend, Pandora's ‘box’ was actually a large storage jar, not a small box.

teile.einleitung: Sharing means letting others have part of something you have. You can share things, but also time and fun. If you share, you make others happy and show that they matter to you.
wichtigste: If you have three apples and your friend has none, you can give one away.
8 jelly bears shared fairly between two makes 4 each.
If two children want the same swing, they can take turns.
You can also share time and fun.
You must not simply take other people's things; you ask first.
You give back a borrowed book carefully.

abschnitte.text: If you have three apples and your friend has none, it is kind to **give away one apple**. Sharing shows that others matter to you. Often sharing makes you happy too. You can share not only food or toys but also **time and fun**. When you play or laugh together, you are sharing something valuable.

When you share fairly, each person gets the same amount. If you share **8 jelly bears** with a friend, each of you gets **4**. If you cut a pizza into **4** equal slices for **4** children, each child gets **1** slice. In maths this is called **division**. You write it, for example, as 8 ÷ 2 = 4.

Some things cannot be divided, for example a **swing**. If two children want to swing at the same time, **taking turns** is a good solution. You can agree how long each child may have. That way everyone gets a turn and there is no quarrel. You can also take turns with a toy or a computer game.

You must not simply take something that belongs to someone else in order to share it. First you **ask** the owner. A polite way to ask is, for example: ‘May I have it, please?’ You look after a **borrowed book** and **give it back carefully**. Then others will be happy to lend you something again.

gewusst: A well-known legend tells how Saint Martin cut his cloak in two with his sword to help a beggar who was freezing.
In many Swiss municipalities St Martin's Day is celebrated on 11 November, for example with lantern processions.

teile.einleitung: Bullying, called ‘Mobbing’ in German, means that someone is deliberately excluded, insulted or tormented over a long period. It can happen at school, at work or on the internet. It is important not to look away and to get help.
wichtigste: Bullying is repeated, targeted harassment of a person.
A single quarrel is not yet bullying.
Bullying by mobile phone and internet is called cyberbullying.
The German word ‘Mobbing’ comes from English.
Bystanders play an important part and can help.
From the 1970s Dan Olweus made bullying in schools widely known.
Getting help is not telling tales, for example at the number 147.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **bullying** when someone is harassed **repeatedly** and **deliberately** over a long period. This can mean laughing at them, insulting them, leaving them out or spreading rumours. A single quarrel is not yet bullying. Typically, the person affected can hardly defend themselves alone. The German word ‘Mobbing’ comes from the English ‘to mob’, which means roughly to crowd round and harass someone. In English, bullying among children is usually simply called ‘bullying’.

When bullying happens via mobile phone and internet, it is called **cyberbullying**. People are shown up, for example, in chats, with photos or comments. This can go on round the clock and reach many people. Those affected should save **screenshots** as evidence and show them to parents or teachers. Then you can block and report the person.

With bullying there are often children who watch but do not step in. They are called **bystanders**. They are important: if they take the side of the person affected, bullying often loses its power. You can stand by the child affected, talk to them or tell an adult. **Getting help is not telling tales**. Children and teenagers can also call the number **147**.

From the 1970s the psychologist **Dan Olweus** studied violence among schoolchildren in **Norway** and **Sweden**. He developed a well-known programme against bullying in schools. Bullying also exists among adults at work. If it comes from a boss, it is called **bossing** in German, from the English word boss.

In the **No Blame Approach** nobody is blamed. The teacher forms a support group, which also includes those involved, and together they look for a solution. The aim is for the bullying to stop without punishing anyone. In **peer mediation**, pupils are trained to settle quarrels among people of their own age. ‘Peers’ are people of the same age.

gewusst: The behavioural scientist Konrad Lorenz used the word ‘mobbing’ for animals that band together in a group against an enemy.
Bullying often stops more quickly when several children say together that they do not think it is all right.

teile.einleitung: Quarrels are part of life, because people do not always want the same thing. What matters is how a conflict is resolved. By talking, listening and finding fair solutions, a quarrel can end well.
wichtigste: In a quarrel, talking to each other helps most.
While the other person is explaining, you listen carefully.
An I-message says how you feel yourself, without blaming.
In a compromise both sides give way a little.
Hitting is never a good solution.
A short break helps you calm down.
A mediator or a teacher can help find a solution.

abschnitte.text: The most important thing in a quarrel is to **talk to each other**. Each side explains what is bothering them and what they would like. While the other person is speaking, you **listen** and do not interrupt. That way you understand better why the other person is angry or sad. Often you realise that it was only a misunderstanding.

An **I-message** says how you feel yourself. It begins, for example, with ‘I feel …’ or ‘I am sad when …’. A you-message such as ‘You're mean!’, on the other hand, sounds like an accusation. The other person feels attacked and defends themselves. With I-messages the conversation stays calmer and fairer.

When you are very angry, a **short break** helps. You breathe deeply, walk a few steps or count slowly to ten. That way you **calm down** and can think more clearly afterwards. **Hitting**, kicking or calling names is never a good idea. Violence only makes a quarrel worse and hurts others.

Often there is a solution that both are happy with. If two children want to read the same book, they can **read it together** or take turns. When both give way a little, this is called a **compromise**. Sometimes you can even find a solution in which both win. What matters is that nobody feels unfairly treated in the end.

Not every quarrel can be solved alone. Then a **teacher** or another adult can help. A person who helps people in a quarrel to reach an agreement is called a **mediator**. The technical term for this is **mediation**. Some Swiss schools have trained pupils who help with quarrels among children of their own age.

gewusst: The word ‘compromise’ comes from Latin and originally meant ‘a mutual promise’.
The idea of the I-message was made known by the American psychologist Thomas Gordon.

teile.einleitung: Responsibility means answering for what you do and its consequences. It begins with small things, in the family and at school, and goes as far as caring for nature and future generations. Swiss law also sets out who is responsible for what.
wichtigste: Anyone who takes responsibility stands by their actions and deals with the consequences.
In Switzerland juvenile criminal law applies from a person's 10th birthday.
In Switzerland you come of age at 18, and have done since 1996.
Anyone who does not help a person whose life is in danger, although it could reasonably be expected, commits an offence.
In 1979 Hans Jonas wrote the book ‘The Imperative of Responsibility’.
In diffusion of responsibility, nobody in a large group feels it is their job.

abschnitte.text: The German word ‘Verantwortung’ is linked to ‘antworten’, to answer: whoever is responsible must be able to answer the question of why they did something. Taking responsibility means **answering for the consequences**. This also includes admitting mistakes and putting them right where possible. You are responsible for yourself, for other people, for animals and for things you use.
