If a school class borrows a piece of equipment, **everyone who uses it** is responsible for it. They handle it carefully and report any damage. Shared responsibility does not mean that nobody has to bother. But this is exactly where a trap lies: **diffusion of responsibility**. In large groups, everyone thinks someone else will act. That is why sometimes nobody helps, even though many people are watching.

In Switzerland the **Juvenile Criminal Law Act** applies to young people from their 10th birthday. Protection and education come first, not punishment. At 18 you come of **age**; before 1996 you only did so at 20. Adults may, for example, sign contracts themselves. Article 128 of the Criminal Code punishes **failure to offer help in an emergency**: anyone who does not help a person in immediate danger of death, although it could reasonably be expected, commits an offence. Often it is enough to call for help, for example on the emergency number 112.

In 1979 the philosopher **Hans Jonas** wrote the book ‘The Imperative of Responsibility’. He believed that modern technology has become so powerful that people are also responsible for **future generations** and nature. His book became important for environmental ethics. This includes using resources **sustainably**: using only so much that later generations can live well too. Saving energy and avoiding waste are simple examples.

gewusst: Until 1996 people in Switzerland only came of age at 20.
In psychology, diffusion of responsibility is also called the ‘bystander effect’.

teile.einleitung: Everyone sometimes makes mistakes or hurts others, often without meaning to. With an apology you show that you are sorry and clear the way for making up.
wichtigste: You apologise even for an accident.
A good apology includes admitting the mistake.
A real apology has no ‘but’.
You can also make up for damage you have caused.
It is best to apologise as soon as possible.
Forgiving means letting go of your anger.

abschnitte.text: If you bump into someone by accident, you say: ‘Sorry!’ That way the other person knows it was **not on purpose**. An apology shows that the other person matters to you. It helps make sure that nobody stays angry or sad for long. It is best to apologise **as soon as possible**; then the anger passes more quickly.

In a good apology you say **what you did wrong**. For example: ‘I'm sorry I knocked over your tower.’ You look at the other person and mean it honestly. A bad apology would be: ‘Sorry, but it's your fault.’ Anyone who blames the other person in the same sentence is not really apologising. A real apology has **no ‘but’**.

You can also show an apology through actions. If you build a knocked-over tower back up, you **make amends** for the damage. If you have damaged a book, you can help to mend it. That shows you mean it. Words and actions together are often the best apology.

When someone apologises to you, you can say: ‘That's all right, thanks.’ Anyone who **accepts** an apology ends the quarrel. **Forgiving** means no longer holding the mistake against the other person and letting go of your anger. That does both of you good. Sometimes you need a little time for this, and that is fine.

When two people are friends again after a quarrel, this is called **making up** or reconciliation. It often begins with an apology. Afterwards you can play and laugh together again. Quarrels are part of life. What matters is learning how to end them again.

gewusst: The German word ‘Entschuldigung’ actually means freeing someone from their guilt.
In everyday life in Switzerland people also often say ‘Exgüsi’, which comes from the French ‘excusez’.

teile.einleitung: Grief is the feeling people have when they lose someone or something important. It is completely natural and can look very different. There are many customs and kinds of help that support people when they are grieving.
wichtigste: Grief is a natural reaction to a loss.
The Zurich-born doctor Elisabeth Kübler-Ross described stages of dying.
The Swiss psychologist Verena Kast described four phases of grief.
In Europe mourners traditionally wear black.
Offering condolences means expressing your sympathy to those left behind.
A flag at half mast is a sign of mourning.
Hospices and palliative care support seriously ill people at the end of their lives.

abschnitte.text: **Grief** arises when you lose something or someone that was important to you. This can be a person, a pet or even a home when you move house. People who are grieving can be sad, angry, tired or confused. Sometimes the feelings change quickly. There is no right or wrong way to grieve, and it helps to talk about it with people you trust.

The doctor **Elisabeth Kübler-Ross** (1926 to 2004), who was born in **Zurich**, worked with dying people in the USA. She described five **stages of dying**, and her model is often applied to grief too. The Swiss psychologist **Verena Kast** described **four phases of grief**. At the beginning there is often a refusal to accept what has happened; later strong feelings break through. In the end a new relationship with yourself and the world can develop. But the phases do not happen in the same way for everyone.

In Europe mourners traditionally wear **black**, while in some Asian countries white is the colour of mourning. A narrow black band on the sleeve is called a **mourning band**; athletes sometimes wear one too. If a flag is raised only halfway up the pole, it is at **half mast**, a **sign of mourning**. This happens, for example, after the death of important people or after disasters.

When you express your sympathy to those left behind, you **offer your condolences**. The word comes from the Latin condolere, ‘to suffer with’. You can offer condolences in person, with a card or in a book of condolence. Often a simple sentence, or just being there, helps. People who are grieving sometimes need a long time, and patience is important.

abschnitte.titel: Support at the end of life
abschnitte.text: A **hospice** is a place where seriously ill people are cared for and supported at the end of their lives. Their relatives are supported there too. **Palliative care** is care that no longer aims to cure, but above all **relieves pain** and preserves quality of life. The term comes from the Latin pallium, cloak. Children and teenagers who are sad can also talk to the number **147**.

gewusst: Elisabeth Kübler-Ross wrote the famous book ‘On Death and Dying’, which was translated into many languages.
The word ‘palliative’ recalls a cloak that is wrapped protectively round a person.

teile.einleitung: Conscience is the inner voice that tells us whether what we do is right or wrong. It often makes itself felt as a good or bad feeling and stays with us all our lives.
wichtigste: Conscience judges your own actions as good or bad.
Pangs of conscience arise when you have acted against your own values.
Conscience is shaped by upbringing and experience.
Article 15 of the Federal Constitution protects freedom of religion and conscience.
Switzerland has had civilian service since 1996.
Antigone and Martin Luther are famous examples of acting according to conscience.

abschnitte.text: **Conscience** is the inner awareness of whether your own actions are right or wrong. If you have done something wrong, you often feel **pangs of conscience**. This unpleasant feeling shows that you have acted against your own values. It can lead you to apologise or to make up for something. If you are convinced you have done nothing wrong, you have a **clear conscience**.

Nobody is born with a finished conscience. According to psychology today, it is shaped by **upbringing and experience**. Children learn from parents, teachers and other role models what is right and wrong. Over many years their own conscience forms in this way. Later people also test these rules for themselves and develop their own convictions.

**Article 15** of the Swiss Federal Constitution guarantees **freedom of religion and conscience**. Every person may freely choose and profess their religion and their philosophical beliefs. Nobody may be forced to join a religious community. So this basic right protects what a person believes deep down to be right.

In Switzerland men are obliged to do military service. Since 1996, anyone who cannot reconcile military service with their conscience can do **civilian service** instead. It lasts longer than military service. It is carried out, for example, in hospitals, care homes, schools or in **nature conservation**. In this way people serve the community in a different way.

In the Greek tragedy **‘Antigone’** by **Sophocles**, Antigone buries her brother even though King Creon has forbidden it. The play shows the conflict between conscience and the law of the state. In 1521, at the Diet of Worms, the reformer **Martin Luther** refused to take back his writings. He is said to have declared that his conscience was captive to the Word of God.

gewusst: The famous sentence ‘Here I stand, I can do no other’ is attributed to Luther, but it was probably only handed down in this form later.
Sophocles wrote ‘Antigone’ about 2,400 years ago.

teile.einleitung: Gender equality means that women and men have the same rights and opportunities, in the family, at work and in politics. People in Switzerland fought for this for a long time, and much of the progress is quite recent.
wichtigste: The Federal Office for Gender Equality has existed since 1988.
Big women's strikes took place on 14 June 1991 and 2019.
International Women's Day is on 8 March.
Since 2005 there has been paid maternity allowance.
Since 2021 fathers have had two weeks of paid paternity leave.
In 1999 Ruth Dreifuss was the first female President of the Swiss Confederation.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland women only got the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in **1971**. In 1981 the principle of **equal rights** for women and men was written into the Federal Constitution. In 1958 the lawyer **Iris von Roten** published the book ‘Frauen im Laufgitter’ (Women in the Playpen). In it she criticised the way women were restricted in marriage, at work and in politics. The book caused fierce debates at the time.

Since 1988 there has been the **Federal Office for Gender Equality (FOGE)**. It belongs to the Department of Home Affairs. The office works, for example, for **equal pay** and for combining family and work. Fighting violence is also one of its tasks. Many cantons have their own equality offices.

On **14 June 1991** and again on 14 June 2019, hundreds of thousands of women took to the streets in Switzerland. Among other things they demanded **equal pay**. Since then 14 June has been regarded as the day of the women's strike. Worldwide, **International Women's Day** on **8 March** recalls the struggle for women's rights. It has been marked for more than a hundred years.

After several failed attempts, the people approved **maternity insurance** in 2004. Since July 2005, working mothers have received money for **14 weeks** after a child is born. In September 2020 the people also approved paid **paternity leave**. Since 2021 fathers have been entitled to **two weeks**. This is meant to make it easier for both parents to combine family and work.

In 1984 **Elisabeth Kopp** became the first woman elected to the Federal Council. In 1993 she was followed by **Ruth Dreifuss**, a Social Democrat from Geneva. In **1999** she became the first female President of the Swiss Confederation. Since then several women have held this office. Today women are far better represented in parliaments and governments than in the past.

gewusst: In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden women had to wait until 1990: only a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court gave them the cantonal right to vote.
The motto of the 1991 women's strike was ‘Wenn Frau will, steht alles still’ (when women want, everything stands still).

teile.einleitung: Courage means doing something even though you are afraid, because it is right or important. Being brave does not mean having no fear. And courage is not the same as recklessness.
wichtigste: You show courage if you try something even though you are afraid.
Helping a child who is being picked on is brave.
Running across the road when the light is red is not brave but reckless.
It is brave to say ‘no’ when others want something wrong.
Admitting a mistake takes courage.
The opposite of brave is cowardly.

abschnitte.text: **Courage** means doing something even though you are afraid. If you are afraid of a task and still try it, you are showing courage. Fear is completely normal; brave people feel it too. The opposite of brave is **cowardly**. Someone is cowardly if, out of fear, they do not do something important even though they could.

Not everything that is dangerous is brave. Running across the road when the light is red is **reckless**, because you put yourself in danger for no good reason. Real courage has a good aim, for example helping someone. Reckless people often just want to show off. Brave people think first and judge what they can do.

If a child is being picked on or laughed at, it is brave to **help** them. A clear sentence such as **‘Stop it!’** can make a big difference. Anyone who just watches and does nothing is a **bystander**. But you do not have to put yourself in danger: fetching an adult is brave too. The courage to stand up for others is called **moral courage**.

It takes courage to say **‘no’** when others want something wrong or dangerous. You risk the others laughing at you. **Admitting a mistake** is also brave, because it is uncomfortable. If you admit your mistake, you show honesty and can put it right. Others will then trust you more.

gewusst: The ancient Greeks already counted bravery among the four most important virtues.
The philosopher Aristotle said that bravery lies in the middle between cowardice and foolhardiness.

teile.einleitung: Tolerance means accepting and respecting other opinions, beliefs and ways of life, even if you do not share them yourself. It is an important basis for living together peacefully.
wichtigste: The word tolerance comes from the Latin tolerare, to bear.
In 1689 John Locke wrote a famous ‘Letter Concerning Toleration’.
Lessing's play ‘Nathan the Wise’ is regarded as a work about religious tolerance.
In 1598 the Edict of Nantes granted French Protestants freedom of religion.
The International Day for Tolerance is on 16 November.
According to a widely held view, tolerance ends where the rights of others are violated.
The opposite of tolerance is intolerance.

abschnitte.text: The word **tolerance** comes from the Latin **tolerare**, which means ‘to bear’ or ‘to endure’. A tolerant person accepts other opinions and ways of life, even if they do not share them. The opposite is **intolerance**. In class you show tolerance by **listening** and letting others **finish speaking**. You can still disagree and say so in a friendly way.

For a long time there were fierce struggles between Christian denominations in Europe. In **1598**, with the **Edict of Nantes**, King Henry IV granted the French Protestants, the Huguenots, freedom of religion. It was later revoked, and many Huguenots fled, including to Switzerland. In **1689** the English philosopher **John Locke** wrote a famous **‘Letter Concerning Toleration’**. In it he demanded that the state should not force people's beliefs.

The German poet **Gotthold Ephraim Lessing** wrote the play **‘Nathan the Wise’**. It is regarded as the best-known work about religious tolerance. It contains the **parable of the rings**: a father has three sons and has two rings made that cannot be told apart from the real one. The three rings stand for Judaism, Christianity and Islam. The story invites people to respect each other instead of arguing about which faith is the right one.

Tolerance does not mean accepting everything. According to a widely held view, it ends **where the rights of others are violated**, for example with violence or discrimination. The philosopher **Karl Popper** described the **paradox of tolerance**: a society that tolerates even intolerance without limit could in the end lose tolerance itself. That is why the rule of law protects basic rights for everyone.

On **16 November** the UN celebrates the **International Day for Tolerance**. In Switzerland the Federal Constitution guarantees **freedom of religion and conscience**. In a country with four national languages and many religions, tolerance is especially important. It helps people of different backgrounds to live well together.

gewusst: In engineering, ‘tolerance’ means the permitted deviation from a measurement, for example with screws.
Many Huguenots who fled to Switzerland brought their knowledge with them, for example of watchmaking.

teile.einleitung: Ethics is a branch of philosophy. It asks what good and right action is and how moral rules can be justified.
wichtigste: The word ethics comes from the Greek ‘ethos’, meaning habit, custom and character.
Aristotle made ethics a subject in its own right.
Morality is the practice people live by; ethics thinks about it.
Descriptive ethics describes morality without judging it.
Metaethics examines the meaning of moral statements.
Applied ethics includes, for example, medical, business and environmental ethics.
According to David Hume, an ought does not automatically follow from an is.

abschnitte.text: The word **ethics** comes from the Greek **‘ethos’**. It refers to a person's usual dwelling place, their customs and their character. **Aristotle** is regarded as the founder of ethics as a field of its own. He treated it as a separate discipline alongside logic and physics. His well-known work is called the ‘Nicomachean Ethics’.

In philosophy a distinction is often made between **morality** and **ethics**. Morality is the norms and values a community actually lives by, for example ‘You should not steal’. Ethics is **thinking about morality**. It asks why a rule applies and whether it is well justified. In everyday life, however, the two words are often used to mean the same thing.

**Descriptive ethics** describes which moral ideas apply in a society, without judging them. It works rather like sociology or ethnology. **Normative ethics** asks what we should do. Important approaches are virtue ethics, the ethics of duty and consequentialist ethics. **Metaethics** stands one level above: it examines what words such as ‘good’ mean and whether moral statements can be true.

**Applied ethics** transfers ethical theories to concrete areas of life. These include **medical ethics**, **business ethics** and **environmental ethics**. Typical questions are about fair wages, protecting nature or how we treat animals. In Switzerland, for example, the National Advisory Commission on Biomedical Ethics advises the authorities and the public on human medicine.

In the 18th century the Scottish philosopher **David Hume** noticed that many authors switch from ‘is’ to ‘ought’ without realising it. But an ought does not simply follow from statements about what is. This is called the **is-ought problem**. Another disputed question concerns **ethical relativism**. It says that moral norms only apply relative to a culture. Critics object that then you could no longer condemn, for example, slavery in other cultures.

gewusst: Aristotle was a pupil of Plato and the teacher of Alexander the Great.
The ‘Nicomachean Ethics’ is probably named after Nicomachus, the son or father of Aristotle.

teile.einleitung: Gender roles are ideas about which tasks, jobs or behaviours are seen as typical for women and men. Such role models come from tradition, upbringing and the media, and they change over time.
wichtigste: A role model shows what a society expects of people.
Around 1900 pink was often seen as a suitable colour for little boys.
A househusband runs the household and looks after the children.
More and more fathers work part-time.
On National Future Day, children discover jobs without stereotypes.
In 2025 the Women's European Football Championship took place in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: A **role model** (in the sense of a set of expectations) describes which tasks and behaviours a society expects of people. For a long time, for example, it was thought that men earn money and women look after the household and the children. Role models come from **upbringing, the media and tradition**. They are not laws of nature and can change a great deal. Today many families share the tasks differently.

One example shows how ideas change. Around 1900 **pink** was often seen as a suitable colour for little **boys**. At that time pink was regarded as the little sister of strong red, and red was seen as masculine. The idea of pink for girls only caught on during the 20th century. So colours for boys and girls are a matter of **habit**, not nature.

A **househusband** is a man who mainly runs the household and looks after the children, often while his partner goes out to work. In the past this was seen as a typical woman's role. In Switzerland many people work **part-time**, that is fewer hours than in a full-time job. This makes it easier to combine family and work. More and more fathers are reducing their working hours for this.

Every job should be open to everyone, whatever their gender. That is why there are **gender-neutral** job titles, such as ‘Fachperson Gesundheit’ (healthcare specialist). On **National Future Day**, children in years 5 to 7 often go to work with a parent or someone they know. The idea is that they also discover **untypical jobs**, for example girls in engineering or boys in nursing.

For a long time football was seen as a typical **men's sport**. In summer 2025 the **Women's European Football Championship** took place in Switzerland. Women's EURO 2025 drew many spectators into the stadiums. This shows that sport is for everyone. In ballet, figure skating or Swiss wrestling, too, people of every gender take part today.

gewusst: In Switzerland women only got the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971.
National Future Day takes place every year in November.

tq47zyr.t: National Advisory Commission on Biomedical Ethics

teile.einleitung: The National Advisory Commission on Biomedical Ethics, NEK for short in German, advises politicians and the public in Switzerland on ethical questions in medicine. The Federal Council set it up in 2001.
wichtigste: The Federal Council set up the NEK in 2001.
The NEK is responsible for ethical questions in human medicine.
Its secretariat is based at the Federal Office of Public Health.
It is an extra-parliamentary commission and is independent in what it says.
Individual research projects are reviewed by the cantonal ethics committees, not by the NEK.
In 2019 the NEK recommended the declaration model for organ donation.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Council** set up the NEK on **3 July 2001**. Its full name is the **National Advisory Commission on Biomedical Ethics** (in German, Nationale Ethikkommission im Bereich der Humanmedizin). It is an **extra-parliamentary commission**, that is a federal expert body whose members are chosen by the Federal Council. Its **secretariat** is based at the **Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)** in Bern. In what it says, however, it works **independently** and is not bound by any instructions.

The NEK writes **opinions**, advises the authorities and informs the public. Its mandate expressly includes encouraging **public dialogue** on ethical questions in medicine. It deals, for example, with questions at the end of life, with vaccinations or with **organ donation**. In 2019 it spoke out against the opt-out solution and recommended the **declaration model**: people should be asked regularly to state their wishes on organ donation. But it does not pass any laws.

The NEK comments on fundamental questions, not on individual applications. Specific **research projects involving humans** are reviewed and approved by the **cantonal ethics committees**, on the basis of the Human Research Act. Since **1998** the **ECNH** (in German EKAH) has been responsible for ethical questions of bio- and gene technology in animals, plants and other organisms. It has, for example, dealt with the dignity of plants.

gewusst: In French the NEK is called the ‘Commission nationale d'éthique’, abbreviated CNE.
The ECNH published a much-discussed report on the dignity of plants.

teile.einleitung: Socrates was a philosopher in ancient Athens and is regarded as one of the founders of Western philosophy. He wrote nothing down himself, but held conversations. We know his thoughts mainly through his pupil Plato.
wichtigste: We know Socrates' thoughts mainly through his pupil Plato.
With maieutics, Socrates helped others to bring out knowledge themselves.
The oracle of Delphi is said to have declared that nobody was wiser than Socrates.
An inner voice, the daimonion, held him back from wrong actions.
The thesis is attributed to him: nobody does wrong knowingly.
In 399 BC he was condemned for impiety and corrupting the young.
He died by drinking a cup of hemlock.

abschnitte.text: **Socrates** lived in **Athens** in the 5th century BC. He wrote no books himself, but talked with people in the marketplace about questions such as: what is just? What is a good life? We know his thoughts mainly through his pupil **Plato**, who wrote down many conversations. The writer Xenophon also reported on him.

Socrates usually did not give ready-made answers. He kept asking questions until the people he was talking with reached new insights themselves. This method is called **maieutics**, in English the **art of midwifery**. Socrates compared himself to a midwife: just as she only helps at a birth, he helped others to bring their own knowledge to light. Often his questions also showed that someone knew less than they thought.

The **oracle of Delphi** is said to have announced that nobody was wiser than Socrates. Socrates explained it like this: at least he knew that he knew nothing. This became the well-known saying **‘I know that I know nothing’**. Socrates also spoke of an inner voice that held him back from wrong actions. He called it the **daimonion**.

For Socrates, knowledge and good action were closely linked. The thesis is attributed to him: **nobody does wrong knowingly**. According to this view, anyone who really knows what is good will also act well. Wrongdoing therefore comes from ignorance. This attitude is called **ethical intellectualism**.

In **399 BC** Socrates was put on trial in Athens. He was accused of **impiety** and **corrupting the young**. He was sentenced to death and had to drink a **cup of hemlock**, a drink made from a poisonous plant. Plato's work **‘Apology’** records his speech in his defence before the court. Socrates is said to have refused to escape because he wanted to respect the laws of his city.

gewusst: According to Plato, Socrates' mother was herself a midwife, which is why his comparison fitted especially well.
The poet Aristophanes made fun of Socrates in his play ‘The Clouds’ while Socrates was still alive.

teile.einleitung: Assisted dying is an umbrella term for actions relating to the death of a seriously ill person. The subject is ethically very controversial. Switzerland has its own rules on it, which differ from those of many other countries.
wichtigste: A distinction is made between passive, indirect active and direct active euthanasia, as well as assisted suicide.
Direct active euthanasia is a criminal offence in Switzerland as ‘killing on request’.
Under Art. 115 of the Criminal Code, assisting suicide is only a criminal offence if done for selfish motives.
Passive euthanasia means not starting or stopping life-sustaining treatment.
Exit was founded in 1982, and Dignitas in 1998 by Ludwig A. Minelli.
In 2012 Vaud became the first canton to regulate assisted suicide in hospitals and care homes by popular vote.

abschnitte.text: In **passive euthanasia**, life-sustaining treatment is not started or is stopped, for example artificial ventilation. In **indirect active euthanasia**, painkillers are given that may shorten life as a side effect. The intention is to relieve suffering. Both forms are regarded as permissible in Switzerland if they match the patient's wishes. You can set out your own wishes in an **advance directive**.

**Direct active euthanasia** is forbidden in Switzerland. The Criminal Code punishes it as **killing on request** (Art. 114). **Assisted suicide** is different: under **Art. 115 of the Criminal Code** it is only a criminal offence if someone acts for **selfish motives**, for example out of greed. What matters is that the person concerned carries out the final act themselves. The Swiss assisted dying organisations base their work on this rule.

The organisation **Exit** was founded in **1982** and is the largest of its kind in Switzerland. In **1998** the lawyer **Ludwig A. Minelli** founded the organisation **Dignitas**, which also accompanies people from abroad. In **2012** voters in the canton of **Vaud** were the first to approve rules on assisted suicide in hospitals and nursing homes. In September 2024 a new, controversial device was used for the first time in the canton of **Schaffhausen**, after which the authorities opened criminal proceedings.

Assisted dying is much discussed in society. Supporters stress a person's **self-determination** over the end of their life. Critics fear that ill or old people could feel under pressure. Many religious communities also view assisted dying critically. An important alternative is **palliative care**, which relieves pain and accompanies people at the end of their lives. Anyone who has worries can find help: children and teenagers, for example, on the number **147**, and adults with Die Dargebotene Hand (the Swiss helpline) on **143**.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the few countries where assisted suicide is allowed under certain conditions.
Exit only accompanies members who live in Switzerland or have Swiss citizenship.

teile.einleitung: Human rights are rights that every person has, simply because they are human. The most important foundation is the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948. Binding treaties followed later.
wichtigste: The UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948.
The Declaration is a resolution and is not binding under international law.
Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the commission that drew up the Declaration.
Human rights are regarded as universal, inalienable and indivisible.
They are often divided into three generations.
The UN Human Rights Council was founded in 2006 and is based in Geneva.
In 1992 Switzerland joined the two UN human rights covenants.

abschnitte.text: On **10 December 1948** the UN General Assembly in Paris adopted the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights**. Since then 10 December has been Human Rights Day. The Declaration has 30 articles. It is a **resolution**, that is a recommendation, and is not legally binding. Even so, it has strongly shaped thinking about human rights all over the world.

The Declaration was drawn up by the UN Commission on Human Rights. It was chaired by **Eleanor Roosevelt**, the former First Lady of the USA. She worked hard to make sure that many countries could agree on a shared text. Experts from different cultures took part. Binding treaties only followed later, above all the two **human rights covenants** of **1966**.

Human rights are regarded as **universal**: they apply to all people everywhere. They are **inalienable**: you cannot give them away or sell them, and nobody may take them away from you. And they are **indivisible**: they belong together and must not be played off against each other. The state has the task of respecting and protecting human rights.

Human rights are often divided into **generations**. The **first generation** covers freedoms such as freedom of expression and the right to vote. The **second generation** are economic, social and cultural rights, for example the **right to education** or to health care. The **third generation** includes rights that often belong to peoples or groups, such as the **right to a healthy environment**, to development and to peace.

The **UN Human Rights Council** was founded in **2006** and is based in **Geneva**. It meets in the Palais des Nations and replaced the former Commission on Human Rights. In **1992** **Switzerland** joined the covenant on civil and political rights and the covenant on economic, social and cultural rights, ten years before it joined the UN in 2002. Switzerland had already ratified the **European Convention on Human Rights** in 1974.

gewusst: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is one of the texts that has been translated into the most languages in the world.
Even before it joined the UN, Switzerland hosted many UN meetings in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: Animal ethics asks how humans should treat animals and what consideration they owe them. Philosophers have given very different answers to this. In Switzerland the subject also plays a part in the constitution and in popular votes.
wichtigste: Speciesism is disadvantaging living beings solely because of their species.
Jeremy Bentham asked whether animals can suffer, not whether they can think.
In the 17th century René Descartes regarded animals as machines without souls.
In 1983 Tom Regan founded a rights-based approach.
The three Rs in animal experiments stand for Replace, Reduce, Refine.
Since 1992 the ‘dignity of living beings’ has been in the Federal Constitution.
On 25 September 2022 voters rejected the factory farming initiative by about 63 per cent.

abschnitte.text: In the 17th century the French philosopher **René Descartes** regarded animals as **automata without souls**, that is as machines without consciousness. This view was later sharply criticised. In 1789 the Englishman **Jeremy Bentham**, one of the founders of utilitarianism, wrote that the decisive question is not whether animals can think or talk, but **whether they can suffer**. For him the **ability to suffer** was the reason to take animals into moral account.

The term **speciesism** means disadvantaging living beings solely because of the species they belong to. It was coined in 1970 by Richard Ryder and made well known by the philosopher **Peter Singer**. With his book **‘The Case for Animal Rights’** (1983), the American **Tom Regan** founded a rights-based approach. For him animals have a value of their own and therefore rights. Other philosophers, on the other hand, think it is justifiable to use animals as long as they are treated well.

abschnitte.titel: Animal experiments and the three Rs
abschnitte.text: For **animal experiments**, the **3R principle** is meant to apply. The three Rs stand for **Replace**, **Reduce** and **Refine** (that is, lessening the strain on the animals). The researchers William Russell and Rex Burch formulated it in 1959. In Switzerland a dedicated 3R competence centre promotes these aims. Animal experiments in Switzerland need a permit.

abschnitte.titel: Switzerland and the dignity of animals
abschnitte.text: In **1893** the Swiss people approved the very first popular initiative: it banned **slaughtering without stunning**. In **1992** the **‘dignity of living beings’** was added to the Federal Constitution; it applies to animals, plants and other organisms. Switzerland was one of the first countries with such a concept. On **25 September 2022** voters rejected the **factory farming initiative** by **about 63 per cent**. Opponents pointed to Switzerland's already strict animal welfare law.

gewusst: Bentham's sentence is often quoted in English: ‘Can they suffer?’
Switzerland is one of very few countries whose constitution also speaks of the dignity of plants and other living things.
